description:
Meldrum House stands within its own parkland at Oldmeldrum in Aberdeenshire, on land with a documented history stretching back to 1236, when it was granted to the Barony of Meldrum during the reign of Alexander II. That medieval origin makes Meldrum's estate one of the older documented landholdings among the properties in this collection, even though the house that occupies the site today reflects several later centuries of expansion and remodelling rather than any surviving medieval fabric.

The core of the current house dates to 1625, and it was substantially built out over the following two centuries: two parallel wings were extended to the east, joined by a wall that creates an enclosed courtyard, a layout distinct from the single-block mansion form seen at many comparable Scottish country houses. Through the 17th and 18th centuries, Meldrum House served as the seat of the Urquhart family, whose long tenure on this estate places them among the more established landowning families of this corner of Aberdeenshire.

Meldrum's most significant architectural transformation came in 1836, when James Urquhart of Meldrum commissioned Archibald Simpson — one of the leading Scottish architects of his generation, particularly associated with the development of Aberdeen's granite architecture — to remodel the house in the Jacobean style. Simpson's work added a grand entrance portico and turreted pavilions, giving Meldrum House the imposing, historicist character that defines its exterior today, layered onto the considerably older 17th-century core.

Today Meldrum House operates as a multi-award-winning 4-star hotel set within 240 acres of Aberdeenshire countryside, its golf offering — the Knights Golf Course, laid out within the estate's own parkland and ranked among the top 100 courses in Scotland — forming a central part of its identity as a country estate hotel. It's worth being clear, however, about exactly how that golf course can be accessed: unlike Dalmahoy near Edinburgh or Dalmunzie Castle in Perthshire, both documented elsewhere in this collection, where non-resident golfers can book tee times as members of the general public, Meldrum's Knights Golf Course is reserved specifically for hotel guests staying on 'stay and play' packages, or for participants in pre-booked corporate and society golf days arranged in advance. There is no simple walk-up or independently bookable round available to a golfer who isn't already a guest or part of one of these organised groups.

That distinction matters for anyone comparing golf access across this pilot's several golf-adjacent castle-hotels: Meldrum represents the more restrictive end of that spectrum, where the course functions as a guest amenity and a corporate events product rather than a genuinely open, non-resident-bookable public facility. For travellers specifically seeking a round of golf without an overnight stay in Aberdeenshire, Meldrum House is not the same kind of confirmed public-access opportunity that Dalmahoy or Dalmunzie represent — though as an overnight destination combining genuine 17th-century origins, a distinguished 1836 Jacobean remodelling by Archibald Simpson, and a well-regarded golf course for guests, it remains a substantial and historically grounded country estate hotel in its own right.

Oldmeldrum itself is a small Aberdeenshire town with its own long history, home to Scotland's oldest working distillery site and a quiet rural character typical of this stretch of countryside north of Aberdeen. Meldrum House's position within 240 acres of surrounding parkland gives guests a genuine sense of rural seclusion despite sitting well within reach of Aberdeen and the wider Aberdeenshire coast, making it a natural base for visitors exploring this less-travelled corner of northeast Scotland alongside better-known Royal Deeside destinations further south.

faqs.question: Can I play golf at Meldrum House without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Generally, no. The Knights Golf Course at Meldrum House is reserved for hotel guests on 'stay and play' packages, or for participants in pre-booked corporate and society golf days. Unlike Dalmahoy or Dalmunzie Castle elsewhere in this collection, there is no simple walk-up or independently bookable public tee time for golfers who aren't already guests or part of an organised group.

faqs.question: Who remodelled Meldrum House, and when?
faqs.answer: In 1836, James Urquhart of Meldrum commissioned the architect Archibald Simpson — a leading figure in Aberdeen's granite architectural tradition — to remodel the house in Jacobean style. Simpson's work added a grand entrance portico and turreted pavilions to the house's 17th-century core, giving Meldrum House its current imposing exterior character.

faqs.question: How old is the Meldrum House estate?
faqs.answer: The land was granted to the Barony of Meldrum in 1236, during the reign of Alexander II, making it one of the older documented estates among the properties in this collection. The house itself, however, dates to 1625 at its core, with major expansion and remodelling continuing through the 18th and 19th centuries.

faqs.question: Which family held Meldrum House the longest?
faqs.answer: The Urquhart family held Meldrum House as their seat through the 17th and 18th centuries, a tenure that included commissioning the house's major 1836 Jacobean remodelling by architect Archibald Simpson under James Urquhart of Meldrum, whose additions gave the house the imposing turreted exterior it retains today.
